evidence.title: Scanner sends MCP-Protocol-Version after initialize
evidence.body:
Every request after `initialize` now carries the version the server negotiated (falls back to the requested 2025-06-18 if the answer is missing or not a date). MCP 2025-06-18 Streamable HTTP requires it, and both tool gates (Python and JS) already send it.

Without the header a server can assume 2025-03-26 and serve tools without `outputSchema` or `title`; HISTOR found two live servers that do (isitabizday.com, mcp.apollographql.com), noted on #240. The issuer then signed a thinner definition than a spec-following client, or our own gate, is served.

Effect: any server that fell back shows one digest change on its next scan, so a watch on it fires one drift alert. DeepWiki is unaffected (HISTOR reproduced its signed digests).

Tests: `tests/test_mcp_protocol_version_header.py` (header on every post-initialize request across all sessions of a scan, negotiated version carried, malformed answers including a CRLF value fall back).

evidence.title: Add MCPSTG-SUPP-06: Test signed and publicly logged tool-manifest revisions
evidence.body:
## Gap

Section 3.13 covers rug pulls well, but the tool-manifest pinning it describes ([What to snapshot](https://github.com/OWASP/MCP-Security-Testing-Guide/blob/main/03.%20MCP%20Threats%20and%20Attack%20Patterns/3.13-supply-chain.md#what-to-snapshot)) is local trust-on-first-use: each client hashes whatever `tools/list` returned the first time it connected. No test checks whether manifest revisions are signed by the expected publisher and recorded in a public, append-only transparency log.

That leaves three gaps:

1. **First use is unverified.** If the server is malicious at first contact, the pin locks the malicious manifest in.
2. **First use happens per machine.** Every laptop and CI runner pins separately, so a server can show the reviewer one manifest and a target another, and every local pin still passes. Only a shared log lets clients compare what they were served (split-view detection, as in Certificate Transparency).
3. **A legitimate update looks the same as a rug pull.** A changed hash says something moved, not who published the new revision.

The local hash plus stop-and-ask in What to snapshot stays the baseline control; SUPP-06 grades it Secure, and re-approval is scored under SUPP-05. SUPP-06 proposes signed, logged revisions as an addition on top of it.

## What changed

- **New test `MCPSTG-SUPP-06`** (Medium, Hybrid), written in full to the `test-case-format.md` template. Six lab cases: an unsigned manifest at first use, a signed and logged revision (the positive control), a signed but unlogged revision, a revision from the wrong signer, a split view across two equally-authorized clients, and runtime drift with no new log entry. Three verdicts: Secure (the hash-and-ask baseline, or full signature and log verification), Insecure (the client claims to verify and then accepts a bad envelope), and Not tested (neither control present, or the positive control fails; label per #52). Includes a canonical-form procedure (RFC 8785 JCS + SHA-256), a synthetic envelope example (explicitly non-standard), and pseudocode for the admission check.
- **New subsection** "Local pins are trust-on-first-use" under *Rug pulls and tool-description drift*.
- **Provenance and signing:** a new mechanism-table row, plus a note that package provenance covers the package bytes but not the `tools/list` a remote server returns at runtime.
- **Control matrix** row for malicious servers, rug pulls, and provenance. The drift list, test chains, and the 3.05 rug-pull `Tests:` line now reference SUPP-06.
- **Appendix D:** placeholders `<TEST_USER_B>`, `<LAB_PUBLISHER_IDENTITY>`, `<LAB_OTHER_IDENTITY>`, `<LAB_TLOG>`.
- **Appendix F:** a "Transparency-log client" tool category.
- **Test count** updated to 81 in README, the chapter 3 overview, and `test-case-format.md`.
- New references [30]–[33]: RFC 8785, RFC 9162, Sigstore Rekor, and SEP-3140 (closed 22 Sep 2026 without merge; may return through a working group).

## Scope

Applies to both local stdio and remote HTTP servers. Remote servers are the main case, because their `tools/list` can change without any package publish, so package provenance does not cover it. For local servers it matters when descriptions are generated at runtime or loaded from the network.

## Severity

Medium until a signing mechanism exists. The 2026-07-28 spec defines no signature, digest, or log field for tool definitions, and the MCP Registry does not record or sign them. A hash-and-ask client is graded Secure against the baseline; only a client with neither control is Not tested.

## Review notes

- All examples are synthetic and lab-only, using placeholders per `CONTRIBUTING.md`. The test explicitly says never to write lab entries to a public transparency log.
- Mappings: OWASP MCP04:2025 (and MCP03:2025), CWE-347, CWE-494, and MITRE ATLAS AML.T0010.005. CWE-347 is used instead of CWE-345, which MITRE marks as Discouraged for mapping.
- #16 and #19 also change the test count and the 3.05 `Tests:` line, so whichever merges second will need a count bump.
- SUPP-01 to SUPP-05 are still the generic template text. I've left them untouched here to keep this PR reviewable, and can follow up with separate PRs that make them concrete in the same style.

Addresses the review request from @vermava.

evidence.author: whiteknightonhorse
evidence.text: On the seller side, the hard part is the gap between the offer and the payment. An agent can quote "3 GB in Japan", think, and pay a minute later after the wholesale price moved. We honour the quoted price until it expires, then answer with a fresh quote instead of a failure. How does the kit handle an offer that goes stale before payment?

evidence.author: whiteknightonhorse
evidence.text: Thanks for the full walk-through. Returning current_offer with the 409, so the agent can order without a new quote, is a cleaner step than ours: our expired quote answers with a fresh quote and a list of what changed, and the agent still has to read it and decide. The below-cost rule makes sense for a reseller. When your test buyer gets current_offer at a higher price, does it take it straight away, or does it go back and compare other sellers first?
